### Problem: Largest number {#sec-lang-p3-largest}

::: {.p-statement}
Given $n \le 100$ non-negative integers ($0 \le a_i \le 10^9$), arrange them so that their concatenation is the largest possible number, and return it as a string.

Source: [LC 179 · Largest Number](https://leetcode.com/problems/largest-number/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Sorting the strings in decreasing lexicographic order fails when one number is a prefix of another: `"30" > "3"` as strings, so it puts `30` first and builds `"303"`, but `"330"` is larger. The reliable rule compares the two possible concatenations directly: put $a$ before $b$ when $a + b > b + a$ as strings. An exchange argument (@sec-pf-greedy) shows that swapping any adjacent pair that violates the rule cannot make the result smaller.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Brute force.** Try all $n!$ orders: only for tiny $n$.
2. **Comparator sort.** Sort with "$a$ first iff $a + b > b + a$".

**Why this is a valid ordering.** For strings $a$, $b$ of digits with lengths $|a|$, $|b|$, as numbers $ab = a\cdot10^{|b|} + b$. So
$$
\begin{aligned}
ab > ba &\iff a(10^{|b|} - 1) > b(10^{|a|} - 1)\\
&\iff \frac{a}{10^{|a|} - 1} > \frac{b}{10^{|b|} - 1}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The comparator compares the real number $f(s) = s/(10^{|s|} - 1)$, so it is a strict weak ordering. (Equal-length strings compare as numbers, so string and numeric comparison agree.) This also gives a **key**: sort by `Fraction(int(s), 10**len(s) - 1)`, descending. A third key that works: `s * 20` (every $|a| + |b| \le 20$, and two infinite repetitions $aaa\ldots$, $bbb\ldots$ that differ, differ within the first $|a| + |b|$ characters).
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
#### Python

```{python}
#| label: lang-largest
def largest_number(nums):
    s = [str(x) for x in nums]
    s.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: (b + a > a + b) - (b + a < a + b)))   # negative: a first
    return "0" if s[0] == "0" else "".join(s)

def largest_number_fraction(nums):
    s = sorted(map(str, nums), key=lambda t: Fraction(int(t), 10 ** len(t) - 1), reverse=True)
    return "0" if s[0] == "0" else "".join(s)

def largest_number_repeat(nums):
    s = sorted(map(str, nums), key=lambda t: t * 20, reverse=True)
    return "0" if s[0] == "0" else "".join(s)

def largest_number_brute(nums):
    return str(max(int("".join(map(str, p))) for p in permutations(nums)))

for _ in range(1000):
    nums = [random.choice([0, 1, 3, 9, 10, 12, 30, 34, 121, 5, 98, 989]) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 6))]
    want = largest_number_brute(nums)
    assert largest_number(nums) == largest_number_fraction(nums) == largest_number_repeat(nums) == want

assert largest_number([10, 2]) == "210"
assert largest_number([3, 30, 34, 5, 9]) == "9534330"
assert largest_number([0, 0]) == "0"
assert largest_number([12, 121]) == "12121"
assert "".join(sorted(["3", "30", "34", "5", "9"], reverse=True)) == "9534303"   # plain sort is wrong
```

#### C++

```cpp
string largestNumber(const vector<int>& nums) {
    vector<string> s;
    for (int x : nums) s.push_back(to_string(x));
    sort(s.begin(), s.end(), [](const string& a, const string& b) {
        return a + b > b + a;               // strict: equal concatenations are "tied", not "before"
    });
    if (s[0] == "0") return "0";
    string out;
    for (const string& t : s) out += t;
    return out;
}
```
:::

::: {#fig-lang-p3-largest}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
ln = ["3", "30", "34", "5", "9"]
plain = sorted(ln, reverse=True)
good = sorted(ln, key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: (b + a > a + b) - (b + a < a + b)))
assert "".join(good) == largest_number([3, 30, 34, 5, 9])

def mark(row):
    return {i: "pink" for i, v in enumerate(row) if v in ("3", "30")}

def draw(ax, p):
    V.trace(ax, p, [
        dict(values=ln, index=False, label="input"),
        dict(values=plain, colors=mark(plain), index=False, label="plain", note="".join(plain) + "  wrong"),
        dict(values=good, colors={**mark(good), **{i: "green" for i in range(3)}}, index=False, label="a+b>b+a",
             note="".join(good) + "  right"),
    ], gap=1.5)
V.show(draw)
```

Plain string order puts 30 before 3; the comparator a + b > b + a puts 3 first, because 330 > 303.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time** $O(n\log n \cdot L)$ where $L \le 10$ is the number of digits, because each comparison builds two strings of length $\le 2L$. **Space** $O(nL)$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All zeros: the concatenation is `"00…0"`; return `"0"`.
- Numbers that are prefixes of each other (`12`, `121`) are where plain lexicographic sorting fails.
- In C++ writing `a + b >= b + a` breaks irreflexivity (`comp(a, a)` is true), which is undefined behaviour in `std::sort`.
:::
